text.p: STOCKS GOLD
Dow Jones close Latest spot rate
FTSE-100 close CRUDE OIL
Nikkei-225 latest $24.90 per bbl
The Dow Jones industrial average set its fourth record for the week on Friday, and oil prices soared to the highest levels since the Gulf War.
The dollar rose against the Japanese yen in response to new reports on trade balances, but declined against other major currencies.

In the stock market, solid corporate earnings reports stoked buying on the eve of the ninth anniversary of the Black Monday stock market crash. Saturday marks the ninth anniversary of Oct. 19, 1987, when the Dow plummeted 508.00 points, or 22.61 percent.

On Friday, the Dow closed up 35.03 points at a new high of 6,094.23, surpassing Thursday's record of 6,059.20. It was the Dow's 31st closing high for 1996, coming just days after it closed above the 6,000 mark for the first time Monday.
For the week, the Dow gained 124.85 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,319 to 1,046 on heavy volume of 467 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Among other indices, the Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 3.83 points to 710.82, its fourth record this week. The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 1.91 to 378.32, a new high.

"We have slow economic growth, inflation is not a problem and by and large, companies are hitting or beating earnings estimates," said William LeFevre, a senior market analyst at Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum.
The index of 30-blue-chip stocks would have racked up an even bigger gain, without the downward pressure exerted by Philip Morris -- a key component.
The company's stock sank as tobacco shares were hammered by news that scientists claimed they had established the first direct link on a cellular level between smoking and cancer.
The Nasdaq Composite index was up 0.52 of a point at 1,242.48. The American Stock Exchange index rose 1.64 to 579.03.
In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose 1/32 of a point, or 31 cents per $1,000 face value, leaving its yield unchanged from Thursday's close at 6.80 percent.
Oil prices surged as cold weather blew into the Northeast and traders and U.S. goverment officials worried about low heating oil stocks.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, November crude oil futures closed at $25.79, up 37 cents a barrel and the highest close since January 1991 in the middle of the Gulf War.
Friday's highest traded price was $25.85, beating the $25.70 post-Gulf War high set last April and matched this week.
The latest rally was a continuation of a bullish trend since the end of July that has been led by heating oil and has pushed crude oil prices up by almost 30 percent.
"It's a bullish close," said Rita Beale, an analyst at Fimat USA Futures.
Thomas Blakeslee, a trader and analyst at Cargill Investors Service, attributed Friday's gains to "continued Iraqi tensions, colder weather, lack of government action."
November heating oil gained 1.77 cents a gallon to 74.06 cents.

In currency markets, the dollar closed at 112.53 yen, up from 112.20 yen late Thursday after Japan's Ministry of Finance reported the Japanese trade surplus tumbled 30.3 percent to 779.52 billion yen in September from a year earlier.
But the dollar dropped against other major currencies, including the German mark. The U.S. currency ended at 1.5424 marks vs. 1.5430 marks late Thursday.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 ended 11.0 points higher at 4,053.1, surpassing its previous record close of 4,050.8 set Tuesday. In Tokyo, the benchmark Nikkei 225 ended 188.56 points higher at 21,612.30.
